name: Bloodletting for leanness

lead: Bloodletting is the removal of blood for health purposes, one of the oldest medical practices, drawn from humoral theory in which health depended on the balance of four bodily fluids. Fringe circles have revived the idea for body composition, with the hope of looking leaner or having a cleaner physique.
Modern medicine uses supervised therapeutic phlebotomy for specific conditions such as hemochromatosis and polycythemia. No published trials have tested it as a way to lose fat or look leaner.

paras: Historically it involved cutting a vein or using leeches or cupping. Modern clinical phlebotomy is done by trained staff in healthcare settings, and blood donation is the everyday form. This article does not describe do-it-yourself methods.
Documented harms include significant blood loss, infection, hematoma, anaemia and hypovolaemic shock. Self-performed bloodletting carries the same risks without clinical supervision.

chain: Blood removed on a traditional or fringe rationale
Claimed to rebalance or 'clear' the body
angle.text: Practitioners of the revived idea hope that removing blood will leave them leaner or healthier-looking. No trial has tested bloodletting for fat loss or appearance.

lead: Bloodletting is the removal of blood for health purposes, one of the oldest medical practices in the world. It was carried out in ancient Egypt and Greece and through medieval Islamic, Talmudic and Ayurvedic medicine, and it was among the most common treatments from antiquity to the late nineteenth century. Under humoral theory, practitioners held that illness came from an imbalance of blood, phlegm, black bile and yellow bile, with an excess of blood (plethora) treated by taking some away.[1]

In a looksmaxxing context the idea has been revived in some fringe circles as a route to a leaner or "cleaner" body. Users who discuss it reason that the body spends energy replacing lost blood and that removal rebalances or purifies the system, so that the result is a leaner-looking physique. These claims circulate in forum discussion; they are not part of modern clinical practice, and no published trial has tested bloodletting for fat loss or appearance.

Today therapeutic phlebotomy is a standard treatment for hemochromatosis and is also used for polycythemia, porphyria cutanea tarda and some other conditions, performed by trained staff.[1][2] Blood donation is the everyday, supervised form, and related traditional practices such as leech therapy, wet cupping and acupoint bloodletting continue in some medical systems and have their own research literatures.[3][4][5]

paras: Historically bloodletting was done by venesection (opening a vein), arteriotomy, scarification with a spring-loaded scarificator, fire cupping or leeches.[1] In the revived fringe version, the appeal is conceptual: blood is treated as something the body must rebuild, so taking it is imagined to raise energy use, shed water or clear impurities. Forum accounts present this as a way to look leaner or more defined; they are not accompanied by measurements, and this article does not describe do-it-yourself methods.

Passages in the Ebers Papyrus suggest bloodletting by scarification was accepted practice in ancient Egypt, and burials there have reportedly contained instruments.[1] Hippocrates mentioned bloodletting but relied mainly on diet, and in the second century Galen promoted physician-directed bloodletting, teaching that blood was made and used up rather than circulating and that health depended on balancing four humours.[1] He gave detailed rules for how much to remove by age, constitution, season, weather and location, and linked particular veins to particular organs.[1]

The Talmud recommended particular days for bloodletting, medieval charts aligned bleeding sites with planets and zodiac signs, and Islamic physicians including Ibn Sina and al-Zahrawi recommended it, especially for fevers, timed by season and the phases of the moon.[1] Hans von Gersdorff's 1517 surgical manual illustrated venesection points on "wound men", helping to teach the procedure to surgeons.[1]

William Harvey's 1628 demonstration of the circulation of the blood undercut the theory behind the practice, but bloodletting became a central technique of 18th-century "heroic medicine".[1] George Washington died in 1799 after roughly 124 to 126 ounces of blood were removed in ten hours; Benjamin Rush was a leading advocate of aggressive bleeding in the United States.[1] Leech use peaked in the 1830s and 1840s, when France imported about 40 million leeches a year.[1]

In the 1830s Pierre Charles Alexandre Louis used statistical methods to show that bleeding did not help in pneumonia and fevers.[1] Resistance continued: in 1871 the British Medical Journal called for a fair trial, William Osler defended it from the 1880s, and a 1923 textbook edition still recommended it.[1] A 2015 study by Helena Miton and colleagues, summarised by Wikipedia, found bloodletting in 60 cultures in the Human Relations Area Files and suggested it may have arisen independently many times as a "cultural attractor".[1]

Therapeutic phlebotomy is the mainstay of treatment in hemochromatosis, where scheduled draws remove red cells and the iron they carry; a typical session removes about 450 to 500 mL, with frequency set by iron levels, and targets are normal serum ferritin and transferrin saturation.[2] It is also used in polycythemia vera, porphyria cutanea tarda, sickle cell disease and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease.[1] A randomised controlled study in 274 patients examined the metabolic and hepatic effects of bloodletting in dysmetabolic iron overload syndrome, a condition defined by raised iron stores, so the setting is iron overload rather than body-composition change.[6]

Physicians also use venipuncture to treat raised hematocrit in men on testosterone therapy, which can raise hemoglobin in a third to a half of users.[7] Blood donation, the commonest form, is standardised: a unit is about 450 mL, donors wait 56 days between whole-blood donations in the US because red cells take an average of 36 days to be replaced, and donors are screened for hemoglobin, blood pressure and pulse.[8]

Leeches remain in use in some surgical, dental and skin settings, and their saliva contains anticoagulant and other bioactive proteins; a 2013 review describes use in plastic and microsurgery to relieve venous congestion in replanted digits and flaps.[3] Wet cupping (hijama) draws blood through small skin incisions and is practised in Unani and Islamic traditions; a review of its proteomic effects summarised eight studies and noted that the effects have not been adequately investigated.[4][9] Traditional East Asian medicine uses acupoint bloodletting, and a 2024 meta-analysis of 17 randomised trials reported improvements on neurological and motor scales in acute stroke.[5]

Proponents of the revival make a small number of connected claims: that the body expends energy to regenerate blood and so burns more, that periodic removal clears the system or reduces puffiness, and that older cultures understood something modern medicine abandoned. They cite the long history of the practice as support.

Clinicians and researchers describe the history differently, noting that mainstream medicine moved away from general bloodletting in the nineteenth century and now reserves phlebotomy for specific conditions such as iron overload and polycythemia.[1] No study has measured fat loss or appearance changes from bloodletting. For donation, authorities describe a cost to the donor in time for red cells to be replaced, and iron supplementation is reported to raise hemoglobin and iron stores in donors, though long-term effects without measuring iron stores are unknown.[8]

Documented harms of bloodletting include significant blood loss, infection and sepsis, hematoma, anaemia and fatal hypovolaemic shock.[1] The Washington case is the best-known historical example of lethal over-bleeding.[1] In blood donation, fainting is the commonest significant reaction, with first-time donors, teenagers and women at higher risk; bruising at the needle site is the commonest minor complaint.[8] Wet cupping and fire cupping carry risks of burns, scarring, infection and skin discolouration.[9] Self-performed bloodletting carries these risks without clinical screening, sterile technique or monitoring, and the wiki does not describe methods.

No studies found on bloodletting for leanness or body composition. Clinical research on related practices addresses other conditions: a 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 randomised trials of bloodletting for acute stroke recovery reported improvement on the NIH Stroke Scale (mean difference -2.08) and in motor function, with the effect on daily living activities not significant overall;[5] a 2017 randomised study in 274 patients examined bloodletting in dysmetabolic iron overload syndrome;[6] and a 2013 review describes leech applications in microsurgery.[3] These studies concern disease settings, not appearance.

lore.intro: On fringe corners of looksmaxxing forums, bloodletting appears as an old technique rediscovered for leanness; clinicians and historians describe it as a largely abandoned practice with narrow modern uses.[1][2]
